newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea to summon president's son over scandal.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea to summon president's son over scandal.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors said on Tuesday they would summon President Kim Young-sam's son for questioning over a loans-for-kickback scandal involving the failed Hanbo Steel Co.
Earlier on Tuesday, Kim Hyun-chul, the president's second son, lodged a criminal libel complaint with the prosecutors saying that six opposition politicians had defamed him over the loan scandal.
"The prosecution will decide exactly when to summon Kim Hyun-chul after reviewing his complaint," a prosecution official told Reuters.
Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung said in parliament: "The Hanbo incident must be investigated thoroughly and those who violated laws should be punished regardless of their social status."

Kim Hyun-chul said five members of parliament from the main opposition National Congress for New Politics and another party official had accused him of influence-peddling in giving loans to Hanbo without any evidence. He has told reporters that he had nothing to do with the loans.
The steelmaking flagship of the Hanbo Group, South Korea's 14th-biggest conglomerate, was declared insolvent on January 23 after racking up five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in loans.
The five opposition legislators include National Congress spokesman Chung Dong-young, and his deputy Sul Hoon.
The president's son had kept the nation waiting on his widely publicised complaint, which he earlier said would be delivered on Monday.
Prosecutors have said the investigation would first focus on the libel complaint against the opposition members, but added it would also look into allegations made against Hyun-chul.
National Congress, which has accused Hyun-chul of playing a key role in brokering loans to Hanbo, blasted his action.
"The whole public has questions for him. If he is so innocent he should appear at a parliamentary hearing to answer questions over the loans," a National Congress statement said.
South Korea's parliament on Monday confirmed it would open a separate probe into the collapse of Hanbo after opposition accusations that prosecutors are not revealing all they know about the scandal.
Speculation that Hyun-chul maintained close links with Hanbo was fanned by Saturday's discovery of more than 10,000 copies of a book written by him in a Hanbo Group warehouse in Seoul.
The opposition has said the books found in the warehouse highlighted that Hanbo had been a sponsor of Hyun-chul.
Hyun-chul would be the first son of an incumbent South Korean president to be summoned for questioning by prosecutors.
The Hanbo scandal has already tarnished President Kim's "Mr Clean" image and dragged his popularity through the gutter.
State prosecutors said they planned to give an interim report on Wednesday on their investigation into the scandal.

Those held in custody over the scandal are a former cabinet minister and three legislators from the ruling party -- two of them Kim's top loyalists -- one opposition member of parliament, two bankers, the founder of Hanbo Group and his former executive.
